analytical_question: Does the cited broad AI-use evidence support the claim that Agentic AI for e-commerce customer-service resolution has reached mainstream diffusion, and what confidence or timing implication is justified?
general_et_finding: Diffusion-stage judgment: indeterminate for Agentic AI generally; confidence is low because there is no representative, longitudinal adoption series or defensible denominator. Rogers categories: innovators—first deployments may represent innovators, but the sources do not identify adopter timing sufficiently to classify them; early adopters—selected named deployments are consistent with early-adopter activity, but this remains a case-level inference, not a population share; early majority—unclassifiable; late majority—unclassifiable; laggards—unclassifiable. General-technology characteristics: relative advantage—possible but not established across uses; compatibility—depends on systems/data and is not measured generally; complexity—case implementations suggest meaningful integration effort, but general complexity is unmeasured; trialability—no representative evidence; observability—public examples exist, but broad observable outcomes/continued use are not established. A broad AI-use rate cannot establish Agentic AI diffusion or an S-curve.
application_finding: Specific application: the evidence shows selected retail deployments with adjacent capabilities (support routing/resolution, order tracking, returns), but not the case's exact bounded delivery-status plus policy-limited refund/replacement workflow or its continued use. Industry/peer diffusion: for e-commerce retailers, the named examples are selected large firms with no denominator, representative sample, or comparable-peer time series; the industry's Rogers stage is indeterminate. Application/peer adopter categories: innovators—some selected deployments could be innovators, but deployment timing is insufficient to verify this; early adopters—named early-use examples are consistent with this group, but this is not a population classification; early majority—unclassifiable; late majority—unclassifiable; laggards—unclassifiable. Application characteristics: relative advantage—plausible but no independent outcomes for this exact workflow; compatibility—one case reports order-management APIs/data assets, not broad compatibility; complexity—multi-month build and specialist partner involvement suggest complexity; trialability—focused initial use cases suggest a bounded start, but no population trial rate; observability—public case accounts but no broad peer outcome measures. Vendors/integrators appear as change agents and complementary assets; no independent trusted opinion leader is identified. One case reports MCP use, which is not evidence of sector-wide standards uptake. Accuracy/reliability and cost are reported broad-AI inhibitors; their specific importance for autonomous refund/replacement actions is an inference.
organization_specific_finding: No posture, deployment history, capabilities, or adopter behavior are supplied for hypothetical retailer C. Its organization-specific timing implication is therefore indeterminate. Do not classify it as an innovator, early adopter, fast follower, or conservative adopter from the broad survey claim.

evidence.claim: BTOS reported that around 14% of Retail Trade businesses used AI in the period ending May 3, 2026, and around 17% expected to use AI in the following six months; the broad AI observation does not establish Agentic AI or customer-service adoption.
evidence.source_or_reference: U.S. Census Bureau, “Large Firms With at Least 20 Employees Biggest AI Users” — https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2026/05/ai-use-businesses.html
evidence.evidence_type: Government survey, nationally representative U.S. business measure
evidence.notes: Population is U.S. Retail Trade businesses, not specifically e-commerce; technology is AI broadly; application is any business function; measure is reported use during the prior two weeks and expected use over six months, not agentic production use or continued use. This is the weak claim under test.

evidence.claim: Two named retailers report customer-service-related agent deployments: Walmart says agents in its Customer Support Assistant route and resolve issues and are increasingly acting autonomously; a Crocs/Salesforce case account describes a customer-facing multi-agent service implementation covering order tracking and returns.
evidence.source_or_reference: Walmart Corporate, “Inside Walmart’s Strategy for Building an Agentic Future” — https://corporate.walmart.com/news/2025/05/29/inside-walmarts-strategy-for-building-an-agentic-future ; Salesforce, “How Crocs built a retail superagent with Agentforce” — https://www.salesforce.com/customer-stories/crocs/building-ai-agents/
evidence.date_or_recency: Walmart published May 29, 2025; Salesforce Crocs case dated September 10, 2026.
evidence.evidence_type: Company deployment statement; vendor-published customer case
evidence.notes: Walmart describes its own system but gives no denominator, service geography, independent evaluation, or sustained-use rate. Salesforce reports a vendor-supported Crocs customer-ready implementation and three agents built in five months, with a voice Help Agent built/launched in seven weeks; user denominator, deployment geography, independently audited outcomes, and continued use are not reported. These are selected cases, not prevalence estimates.

evidence.claim: In a survey of 56 AI leaders at U.S.-based NRF member retailers, cost and model accuracy/reliability were each cited by 57% as top AI strategic concerns; 55% cited workforce AI expertise gaps.
evidence.source_or_reference: National Retail Federation Center for Digital Risk & Innovation, “Retail AI Trends 2025” — https://nrf.com/research/retail-ai-trends-2025
evidence.evidence_type: Industry association survey of selected retailer AI leaders
evidence.notes: Respondents were contacted through NRF councils/working groups; the small self-reported sample is not representative of all retailers. It concerns AI broadly and does not measure Agentic AI or this customer-service application. Reliability is a particularly relevant inhibitor for action-taking service, but that application-specific emphasis is an inference.

evidence.claim: The assigned Chapter 6 framework treats diffusion as social, distinguishes decision stages, describes approximate Rogers adopter categories and five innovation characteristics, and cautions that curve fitting depends on good adoption data and a defensible population denominator.
evidence.source_or_reference: Andres Fortino, Mastering the Craft of Emerging Technology Adoption, Chapter 6, “The Diffusion of Emerging Technologies,” pp. 77–90 (assigned course text).
evidence.notes: This is the conceptual framework, not current empirical evidence about Agentic AI adoption.

contrary_evidence_or_limitations: No cited source provides a representative Agentic AI adoption rate, installed base, market share, or longitudinal curve for retail customer-service resolution.

The broad Census measure includes any AI function, while the proposed application requires agentic actions; it cannot support the specified technology/application adoption percentage or a Rogers category.

The two named retailer examples are large, selected organizations; one is a vendor customer story. They do not show the experience of a representative retailer population, common e-commerce workflows, or sustained use.

The application examples are adjacent rather than exact: the evidence does not establish routine delivery-status handling plus bounded refunds/replacements with human escalation as a standardized, commonly adopted use.
The NRF survey is selected and self-reported and concerns AI generally. It supplies inhibitor context, not direct diffusion evidence for Agentic AI.
confidence_and_uncertainty: High confidence that the cited Census figure is insufficient to support the claim because its population, technology, application, and measurement differ. Low confidence in the actual Agentic AI customer-service diffusion stage because representative and longitudinal data are missing. This means the stage is not classifiable from available evidence, not that adoption is necessarily low.
value_opportunity_implication: Confidence is high that the Census statistic is misapplied to the claimed technology and application because its population, technology, application, and measure differ. Confidence is low about the actual Agentic AI customer-service diffusion stage: no representative or longitudinal data are provided. Do not replace the unsupported claim with the opposite claim that adoption is necessarily low.
risk_governance_implication: The Census data do not support the stated mainstream-diffusion claim. They cover U.S. Retail Trade businesses, not specifically e-commerce firms; AI broadly, not Agentic AI; and any business function, not customer-service resolution. Expected use is intention rather than actual use. The source's two-week use measure also does not establish continued adoption. The named company examples are not a representative sample.
recommendation_management_implication: The 14% broad-AI statistic cannot show that the specified application is mainstream, that retailer C is behind, or that it should act now. The agent abstains from assigning a confident Rogers stage for either the exact technology/application pair or the organization. Monitor for direct, dated, comparable evidence; no adoption decision is made.
change_monitoring_triggers: A dated, representative survey of e-commerce retailers that separately measures Agentic AI customer-service deployments, distinguishes pilots from production, specifies a denominator and geography, and tracks continued use or abandonment.
Independent or audited outcomes from multiple retailers for autonomous routine resolution, including accuracy, escalation, refund/return error rates, customer outcomes, and operating cost.
Repeated evidence of adoption across retailers of different sizes and system architectures, rather than additional announcements from a few large firms.
Comparable peer evidence on interoperability, standards use, integration effort, and actual production deployment.
abstention_or_more_information_needed: Do not assign Agentic AI generally or this exact application to early majority, late majority, or laggards without representative adoption data and a defined population denominator.
Request direct e-commerce customer-service evidence that distinguishes agentic resolution from conventional chatbots, human-assist tools, and general AI use.
Request the target geography, comparable retailer population, deployment status, and continuation/abandonment evidence before estimating diffusion proportions or curve position.
